# Upgrade procedures

<Note>

This page applies to Terraform Enterprise only. HashiCorp operates and upgrades HCP Terraform. For HCP Terraform, focus on keeping self-hosted agents current, as described in [Identity and access management](/validated-designs/terraform/administration-guide/identity-and-access-management#upgrading-hcp-terraform-agents).

</Note>

Terraform Enterprise upgrades are routine operations, not projects. Teams that upgrade rarely accumulate several intermediate releases, larger database migrations, and more breaking changes per upgrade, which makes each upgrade riskier and longer. We recommend that you upgrade on a regular, scheduled cadence so that you stay on a supported release, receive security fixes promptly, and keep each upgrade small. Write the procedure down as a runbook, and have someone other than its author test it so that more than one member of the platform team can run it.

The authoritative procedure is <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/upgrade" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">Upgrade Terraform Enterprise</a>. This page adds the operating practices around it.

## Test in a non-production mirror first

Maintain a non-production Terraform Enterprise instance that mirrors production: same operational mode, runtime, operating system, external services, network path, proxy and CA configuration, and deployment code. Run every upgrade there first, from the same artifacts and runbook you will use in production, and run a representative set of workspaces (including VCS-driven runs, agent pools, policy sets, and run tasks) before you promote the upgrade. The same instance serves as the platform team's environment for testing agent versions and policy changes, as described elsewhere in this guide.

## Plan the upgrade

1. Select the target version and review the release notes for it and every intermediate release for breaking changes, deprecations, and new requirements.
1. Identify required intermediate releases and stage the container images for each in your internal registry. This is especially important in air-gapped environments, where you should also stage the matching Terraform binaries and provider versions.
1. Schedule a maintenance window. The standard procedure takes Terraform Enterprise offline; in field upgrades of a single instance, the application was unavailable for minutes, but database migrations for larger version jumps can take considerably longer. Measure the duration in your mirror environment and size the window from that.
1. Define rollback criteria and rehearse the rollback, including restoring PostgreSQL, object storage, and configuration from backup.
1. Notify consumer teams and freeze automation that could start runs during the window.

## Run the upgrade

1. Gracefully drain work from each node so active runs complete and no new runs start. Refer to the <a href="https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/enterprise/deploy/manage/upgrade" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer">upgrade documentation</a> for the drain command for your runtime.
1. In active/active mode, scale down to a single node. Active/active mode does not provide zero-downtime upgrades. If an autoscaling group or orchestrator manages the nodes, disable health checks that would replace instances during the upgrade.
1. Stop the application and back up PostgreSQL, object storage, Redis (where used), and configuration, including the encryption password.
1. Change the Terraform Enterprise version in your deployment code and apply it. With the HashiCorp Validated Design deployment modules, this means updating the image version in your variables file and applying the change; with Helm, update the image tag in your values file and run `helm upgrade`. Avoid manual changes on the host, so that the deployment code remains the source of truth.
1. Start the application, wait for database migrations to complete, and scale back to your target node count.

## Validate

After the upgrade, verify the following before you reopen the platform:

- The health check and startup checks pass.
- Users can sign in through SSO, and team mapping still works.
- A VCS-driven workspace receives a webhook and completes a plan.
- A run on a self-hosted agent pool completes, and agent versions are compatible with the new release.
- Policy sets and run tasks evaluate as expected.
- Logs and metrics are still forwarded to your observability platform.

Record the actual duration and any issues in the runbook so that the next upgrade is faster.
